title: Going Concern Analysis
answer: Going concern analysis is the assessment of whether an entity can continue operating and meet its obligations for the foreseeable future. In continuous audit and assurance, it is not a single annual judgment but an ongoing review of liquidity, cash flow, debt maturities, covenant compliance, and access to capital. It supports audit conclusions, management planning, lender communications, and investor disclosure. The work sits inside The AI Accountant's continuous audit and assurance field, where financial and non-financial signals are monitored between reporting dates.

sections.body: Going concern analysis is the assessment of whether an entity can continue operating and meet its obligations for the foreseeable future. In continuous audit and assurance, it is not a single annual judgment but an ongoing review of liquidity, cash flow, debt maturities, covenant compliance, and access to capital. It supports audit conclusions, management planning, lender communications, and investor disclosure. The work sits inside The AI Accountant's continuous audit and assurance field, where financial and non-financial signals are monitored between reporting dates.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The analysis runs on data from the general ledger, enterprise resource planning systems, treasury workstations, bank feeds, debt schedules, covenant certificates, and cash flow forecasts. External inputs can include filings, credit market data, news, and industry indicators. In an AI-assisted setup, these sources are ingested into a governed data layer, normalized, and refreshed on a schedule. Models, rules, and dashboards then run on cloud or on-premises infrastructure, with alerts sent to auditors and finance teams when thresholds are crossed.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work combines quantitative measures such as liquidity ratios, cash runway, covenant headroom, debt maturity profiles, and forecast accuracy with qualitative factors such as management plans, customer concentration, supplier reliance, litigation, and regulatory change. AI methods can include anomaly detection, scenario modeling, natural language processing of filings and news, and predictive models for financial distress. Auditors and analysts then challenge assumptions, test the reliability of forecasts, and document their conclusions. Continuous monitoring links these steps to thresholds and triggers, so that a deteriorating signal prompts a fresh review rather than waiting for the next reporting cycle.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Because going concern conclusions can affect audit opinions, lending decisions, and market disclosure, the evidence must be traceable to source systems with timestamps, version history, and clear ownership. Data rights, confidentiality, and contractual limits on bank and customer information shape what can be ingested and who can see it. AI outputs require validation, bias checks, explainability, and human sign-off before they influence a conclusion. Model governance, access controls, and audit trails are therefore part of the analysis, not an afterthought.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Going concern analysis is moving toward more continuous, forward-looking monitoring that connects treasury data, covenant tracking, and external signals in near real time. AI is likely to improve early warning, scenario simulation, and the extraction of risk language from filings and news, while professional judgment remains central to the conclusion. Assurance standards and regulation will continue to adapt to AI-generated evidence and model risk. Progress will depend on data quality, integration across systems, and the willingness of auditors and regulators to trust documented, explainable outputs.
